quests.instruction: You are labeling a kitchen jar. Write the label 'Sugar' with a capital S.
quests.question: Sugar
quests.hint: Capital S, then 'ugar'. g has a tail below the line. Make the letters clear and big enough to read from across a table.
quests.explanation: Labels need to be easy to read at a glance. Clear letters and a capital at the start do the job.
quests.funFact: Sugar cane is a tall grass, and India is one of the biggest sugar producers in the world.

quests.instruction: Label a box of tea. Write 'Tea bags' on two words.
quests.question: Tea bags
quests.hint: Capital T, 'ea', a gap, then 'bags' with a tall b and a tailed g. Only the first word gets a capital.
quests.explanation: On a label, the first word has a capital and the rest are small, unless a word is a name.
quests.funFact: According to a popular story, tea bags were invented by accident when a New York merchant sent tea samples in small silk bags.

quests.instruction: Label a shelf of food. Write 'Rice and lentils'.
quests.question: Rice and lentils
quests.hint: Capital R, 'ice', gap, 'and', gap, 'lentils' with its tall l's and t. Keep the three words even.
quests.explanation: Three words in one label: check the gaps are equal and the baseline is level.
quests.funFact: Rice and lentils are eaten together in many parts of the world, in dishes such as khichdi.

quests.instruction: Write a name label for a notebook: 'Name: Maya'. Put a colon after the word Name.
quests.question: Name: Maya
quests.hint: Capital N, 'ame', then the colon (two dots, one above the other), a gap, then capital M and 'aya'.
quests.explanation: The colon follows the label word and comes before the information. Keep the two dots small and in line.
quests.funFact: The word 'colon' comes from a Greek word that meant a limb, or a part of a sentence.

quests.instruction: Write a class label: 'Class: 4'.
quests.question: Class: 4
quests.hint: Capital C, 'lass', the colon, a gap, and the number 4. The number should be as tall as the capital C.
quests.explanation: A label can use letters and numbers together. Keep the number the same height as the capital letters.
quests.funFact: The school year in India usually begins in April, though some states and schools start in June.

quests.instruction: Write a subject label: 'Subject: English'.
quests.question: Subject: English
quests.hint: Capital S, 'ubject' (tall b, dotted j with a tail), colon, gap, capital E and 'nglish' (tail on g, tall l and h). Check both capitals are tall.
quests.explanation: Two capitals and a colon. This is how real labels on school books are written.
quests.funFact: More than a billion people speak English as a first or second language.

quests.instruction: Write a shopping list with three items in a row: 'milk, eggs, bread'.
quests.question: milk, eggs, bread
quests.hint: Write each item and put a comma right after the first two. Leave a gap after each comma. g has a tail.
quests.explanation: A list is easier to read when the commas touch the word before them and the gaps are even.
quests.funFact: An eggshell has thousands of tiny holes, called pores, that let air in and out.

quests.instruction: Write your list of vegetables: 'rice, onions, tomatoes'.
quests.question: rice, onions, tomatoes
quests.hint: Three items with two commas. The tall letters: d, t, t. Dot on i's after each word.
quests.explanation: Tall letters, dots and commas: lots of details in one line. Write the main letters first, then add the dots.
quests.funFact: In science a tomato is a fruit, because it grows from a flower and has seeds.

quests.instruction: Write a fruit list: 'apples, bananas, grapes'.
quests.question: apples, bananas, grapes
quests.hint: Three plural words. Keep them even and do not let them touch the line below. Remember: tall stems (l, b) reach the top line and tails (p, g) drop below the baseline.
quests.explanation: Plural words often end in s. Keep your s's the same size at the end of each word.
quests.funFact: Grapes can be dried and turned into raisins.

quests.instruction: Write the classroom instruction 'Open your books.'
quests.question: Open your books.
quests.hint: Capital O, then 'pen', gap, 'your' with tails on y, gap, 'books' with b, k tall and two o's. End with a full stop.
quests.explanation: Instructions on a board start with a capital and end with a full stop. Write them clearly so everyone can read them.
quests.funFact: In old libraries, books were sometimes chained to the desks so they would not be taken.

quests.instruction: Write 'Line up quietly.' as it might appear on the board.
quests.question: Line up quietly.
quests.hint: Capital L, 'ine', gap, 'up', gap, 'quietly' with tails on q, y and tall letters t, l. Full stop.
quests.explanation: A three-word instruction. Make sure the tail on q doesn't cross the tall letter of the word below.
quests.funFact: Classroom chalk is often made from a soft rock called gypsum.

quests.instruction: Write 'Please sit down.' as if for a class sign.
quests.question: Please sit down.
quests.hint: Capital P, 'lease', gap, 'sit', gap, 'down' with a tall d. Dot the i. Full stop.
quests.explanation: A polite sentence in three words. Check that capital P and the tall d match in height.
quests.funFact: In the late 1900s whiteboards began to replace chalkboards in many classrooms.

quests.instruction: Write the sign 'No entry'. Capital N for the first word only.
quests.question: No entry
quests.hint: Capital N, 'o', gap, 'entry' with a tall t and y with a tail. Make the letters big and clear, as on a sign.
quests.explanation: Signs use short words and clear letters so people can read them quickly.
quests.funFact: Road signs use shapes and colors so people can understand them quickly, even when they speak different languages.

quests.instruction: Write the warning 'Wet floor'. A sign must be easy to read.
quests.question: Wet floor
quests.hint: Capital W, 'et', gap, 'floor' with a tall f and l. Cross the t and make the o's round.
quests.explanation: Warnings need to be clear. Even, upright letters make them easier to read.
quests.funFact: Wet floors are slippery because a thin layer of water reduces the grip between a shoe and the floor.

quests.instruction: Write 'Please wait here.' as it would appear on a sign.
quests.question: Please wait here.
quests.hint: Capital P, 'lease', gap, 'wait', gap, 'here' with a tall h. Dot both i's and finish with a full stop.
quests.explanation: A three-word sign with a full stop. Keep the baseline level and letters upright.
quests.funFact: What Americans call a line of people waiting, British speakers call a queue.

quests.instruction: Write the reminder 'Feed the cat.' for the fridge door.
quests.question: Feed the cat.
quests.hint: Capital F, 'eed', gap, 'the', gap, 'cat', then a full stop. F and t and h are tall. Keep the e's closed.
quests.explanation: A reminder is short and clear. Capital at the start, full stop at the end.
quests.funFact: Cats cannot taste sweetness.

quests.instruction: Write the reminder 'Water the plants.'
quests.question: Water the plants.
quests.hint: Capital W, 'ater', gap, 'the', gap, 'plants' with a tail on p and tall l and t. Full stop.
quests.explanation: Three words with tall letters in the second and third. Check their heights.
quests.funFact: Plants lose water through tiny holes in their leaves called stomata.

quests.instruction: Write the reminder 'Call Grandma at 5:00.' Add the time with a colon.
quests.question: Call Grandma at 5:00.
quests.hint: Capital C, 'all', gap, capital G, 'randma' (tall d), gap, 'at', gap, 5 colon 00. End with a full stop.
quests.explanation: A reminder with a name and a time. Capitals for the start and the name, a colon in the time.
quests.funFact: Alexander Graham Bell was granted a patent for the telephone in 1876.

quests.instruction: Write a note for the door: 'Gone to the shop. Back soon.'
quests.question: Gone to the shop. Back soon.
quests.correctAnswer: Gone to the shop. Back soon.
quests.hint: Two short sentences: capital G and capital B, full stop after each. Leave a slightly wider gap after the first full stop.
quests.explanation: Two sentences need two capitals and two full stops. This is how real notes are written.
quests.funFact: Sticky notes were invented in the 1970s using a glue that was not very sticky.

quests.instruction: Write the start of a note: 'Dear Mum, I am at school.'
quests.question: Dear Mum, I am at school.
quests.correctAnswer: Dear Mum, I am at school.
quests.hint: Capital D, 'ear', gap, capital M, 'um', comma, gap, capital I, 'am at school'. Full stop at the end.
quests.explanation: A comma comes after the person's name when you start a note. Then the message begins with a capital I.
quests.funFact: India Post is one of the largest postal networks in the world.

quests.instruction: Write a thank-you note: 'Thanks for the book!'
quests.question: Thanks for the book!
quests.hint: Capital T, 'hanks', gap, 'for', gap, 'the', gap, 'book', then the exclamation mark. Remember: tall stems (h, k, f, b) reach the top line.
quests.explanation: A short note with an exclamation mark shows that you are pleased.
quests.funFact: The Library of Congress in the United States is the biggest library in the world by the number of items it holds.

quests.instruction: Write the first line of a daily schedule: '8:00 Wake up'.
quests.question: 8:00 Wake up
quests.hint: Write the time first: 8, colon, 00. Then a gap, capital W, 'ake', gap, 'up' with a tail on p.
quests.explanation: Schedules put the time first. The number should be as tall as the capital letter that follows.
quests.funFact: India uses a single time zone, Indian Standard Time, for the whole country.

quests.instruction: Write a timetable line: 'Mon - Art'.
quests.question: Mon - Art
quests.hint: Capital M, 'on', gap, a short flat dash, gap, capital A, 'rt'. The dash sits at the middle of the letters.
quests.explanation: Mon is short for Monday. A shortened word is called an abbreviation, and it still starts with a capital.
quests.funFact: Hourglasses were used to measure time for hundreds of years before mechanical clocks became common.

quests.instruction: Write a schedule line: '4:30 Play time'.
quests.question: 4:30 Play time
quests.hint: 4, colon, 30, a gap, capital P, 'lay' (tall l, tailed p and y), gap, 'time' with a dot on i and a cross on t.
quests.explanation: The time, then the activity. Two words after the number, with an even gap in each place.
quests.funFact: Playing helps children practise sharing, planning and solving problems.

quests.instruction: Write a birthday greeting: 'Happy Birthday, Maya!'
quests.question: Happy Birthday, Maya!
quests.hint: Capitals H, B and M. A comma after Birthday, an exclamation mark at the end. p and y have tails.
quests.explanation: A greeting has capitals for the main words and the name. The comma separates the greeting from the name.
quests.funFact: The tune of 'Happy Birthday to You' began as a classroom greeting, 'Good Morning to All', written by two sisters in the 1890s.

quests.instruction: Write an invitation line: 'Please come to my party.'
quests.question: Please come to my party.
quests.hint: Write 'Please come', then 'to my party.' The tails of p, y, p and y go below the baseline, so leave room beneath the line.
quests.explanation: A friendly sentence with a few tails. Keep the baseline level and the gaps equal.
quests.funFact: A birthday party invitation written on a wooden tablet nearly two thousand years ago has been found at a Roman fort in Britain.

quests.instruction: Write a closing line: 'Thank you for coming.'
quests.question: Thank you for coming.
quests.hint: Capital T, 'hank', 'you' (tail on y), 'for', 'coming' (tail on g). Full stop at the end.
quests.explanation: A polite line you would really write on a card. Keep the letters round and even.
quests.funFact: The word 'thank' is related to the word 'think'.

quests.instruction: Write a sentence about yourself, as a model: 'My name is Ravi Menon.'
quests.question: My name is Ravi Menon.
quests.hint: Capital M for the first word, capital R and capital M for the name. A full stop at the end.
quests.explanation: A name is made of capitals and small letters. Three capitals in one sentence should all be the same height.
quests.funFact: A signature is a handwritten version of your name, and everyone's looks a little different.

quests.instruction: Write: 'I am nine years old.'
quests.question: I am nine years old.
quests.hint: Capital I, 'am', 'nine' with the dot on i, 'years' with a tail on y, 'old' with a tall l and d. Full stop.
quests.explanation: Five short words. Notice that numbers in sentences can be written as words as well.
quests.funFact: In many countries a baby's age is counted in months at first, then in years.

quests.instruction: Write: 'I am in Class 4, Section B.'
quests.question: I am in Class 4, Section B.
quests.correctAnswer: I am in Class 4, Section B.
quests.hint: Capital I, 'am in', capital C, 'lass', the number 4, a comma, capital S, 'ection', capital B. End with a full stop.
quests.explanation: Capitals and numbers mix in this sentence. Keep each number as tall as a capital letter.
quests.funFact: A code that mixes letters and numbers, like 4B, is called an alphanumeric code.
